subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 24-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand and presents with shoulder pain and deformity. Radiographs show a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. On exam, the lateral aspect of his shoulder appears flattened, he cannot initiate arm abduction past 15 degrees, and there is decreased sensation over the lateral arm.
question: Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?
explanation_correct: The axillary nerve (C5-C6) courses around the surgical neck of the humerus, making it vulnerable in fractures there and in anterior shoulder dislocations. It innervates the deltoid, so injury produces a flattened deltoid contour and loss of arm abduction beyond the first 15 degrees (the supraspinatus initiates the first 15 degrees). It also carries sensation over the deltoid and lateral arm (regimental-badge area). This constellation localizes the lesion to the axillary nerve.

explanation_incorrect.B: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the biceps, brachialis, and coracobrachialis; injury causes loss of forearm flexion and supination with a reduced biceps reflex, not a flattened deltoid or lateral arm sensory loss.
explanation_incorrect.C: The radial nerve is injured in midshaft humerus fractures and causes wrist drop with posterior arm/forearm and dorsal hand sensory loss; it does not abduct the arm at the shoulder.
explanation_incorrect.D: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus; injury affects the first 15 degrees of abduction and external rotation, not abduction beyond 15 degrees or lateral arm sensation.
explanation_incorrect.E: The ulnar nerve is injured at the medial epicondyle and causes clawing of the fourth and fifth digits with ulnar-sided sensory loss, not a shoulder abduction deficit.

educationalObjective: Surgical neck humerus fractures and anterior shoulder dislocations injure the axillary nerve, causing deltoid paralysis and lateral arm sensory loss.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 19-year-old football player sustains a traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus during a tackle. He has weakness of elbow flexion and forearm supination, a diminished biceps reflex, and loss of sensation over the radial (lateral) aspect of the forearm. Shoulder abduction is intact.
question: Which nerve is most directly responsible for the flexion and supination deficit?
explanation_correct: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C7) arises from the upper trunk and innervates the biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis, the primary elbow flexors, as well as providing supination via the biceps. Its terminal sensory branch, the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve, supplies the radial/dorsal forearm. An upper trunk lesion reduces the biceps reflex and weakens flexion and supination, matching this patient.

explanation_incorrect.A: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor and sensation over the lateral shoulder; it does not flex the elbow or carry forearm sensation.
explanation_incorrect.B: The radial nerve extends the elbow, wrist, and fingers; its injury causes wrist drop, not loss of elbow flexion or a diminished biceps reflex.
explanation_incorrect.D: The median nerve flexes the wrist and fingers and innervates thenar muscles; it does not supply the biceps reflex or radial forearm sensation.
explanation_incorrect.E: The ulnar nerve (C8-T1) supplies intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar-sided sensation, not elbow flexion or the biceps reflex.

educationalObjective: Musculocutaneous nerve injury from upper trunk compression produces weakened elbow flexion/supination, a decreased biceps reflex, and radial forearm sensory loss.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 55-year-old man falls asleep in a chair with his arm draped over the backrest. He awakens with inability to extend his wrist and fingers. Examination shows wrist drop and decreased grip strength, with loss of sensation over the posterior forearm and dorsal hand. Triceps strength is normal.
question: Which nerve has been compressed?
explanation_correct: Compression of the radial nerve in the axilla (Saturday night palsy, for example from crutches or an arm over a chair) causes wrist drop, or loss of elbow, wrist, and finger extension, because the radial nerve supplies the extensors. Grip strength is reduced because wrist extension is required for maximal finger flexor action. Sensory loss involves the posterior arm/forearm and dorsal hand.

explanation_incorrect.A: Median nerve injury causes loss of wrist flexion and thenar weakness (ape hand/hand of benediction), not wrist drop.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ulnar nerve injury produces a claw hand and ulnar-sided sensory loss, not wrist drop.
explanation_incorrect.D: Musculocutaneous nerve injury affects elbow flexion and the biceps reflex, not wrist extension.
explanation_incorrect.E: Axillary nerve injury causes deltoid paralysis and lateral arm sensory loss after surgical neck humerus fractures, not wrist drop.

educationalObjective: Radial nerve compression in the axilla causes wrist drop with dorsal hand sensory loss; grip weakness results from loss of wrist extension.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 30-year-old man sustains a midshaft humerus fracture in a motorcycle crash. He develops wrist drop and numbness over the dorsal hand. When asked to extend his elbow against resistance, he does so successfully, and sensation over the posterior arm is normal.
question: Which of the following findings is expected given the level of this lesion?

options.text: Loss of triceps function and posterior arm sensation
Ape hand deformity with loss of thumb opposition
Ulnar clawing of the fourth and fifth digits
Preservation of triceps function and posterior arm sensation
Loss of sensation over the lateral three and a half fingers

explanation_correct: The radial nerve (C5-T1) runs in the spiral groove of the midshaft humerus. Branches to the triceps and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm arise proximal to the spiral groove and are typically spared in midshaft fractures; the radial nerve continues distally to supply the wrist and finger extensors. Thus elbow extension and posterior arm sensation are preserved while wrist drop and dorsal hand sensory loss occur. This distinguishes a midshaft lesion from a more proximal axillary radial nerve injury.

explanation_incorrect.A: Loss of triceps function and posterior arm sensation would indicate a lesion proximal to the spiral groove, such as axillary compression, not a midshaft injury.
explanation_incorrect.B: Ape hand results from median nerve thenar dysfunction, not radial nerve injury.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ulnar clawing reflects ulnar nerve or lower trunk pathology, not radial nerve injury.
explanation_incorrect.E: Loss of lateral three-and-a-half finger sensation is a median nerve deficit, not a radial nerve finding.

educationalObjective: In midshaft humerus fractures, radial nerve injury spares triceps and posterior arm sensation while causing wrist drop and dorsal hand sensory loss.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A child falls and sustains a supracondylar fracture of the humerus. On exam, the child cannot flex the wrist or the lateral two digits and cannot oppose the thumb. When asked to make a fist, the index and middle fingers remain extended. There is loss of sensation over the thenar eminence and the dorsal and palmar aspects of the lateral three and a half fingers.
question: Which nerve is injured?
explanation_correct: Supracondylar humerus fractures classically injure the median nerve, producing a proximal lesion. The median nerve (C5-T1) supplies the LOAF muscles, namely the lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, and flexor pollicis brevis, as well as the wrist flexors. Loss of the lateral two lumbricals prevents flexion of the MCP joints of the index and middle fingers, so making a fist produces the hand of benediction. The sensory loss over the lateral three and a half fingers and thenar eminence is consistent with a proximal median lesion.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ulnar nerve lesions affect the medial one and a half fingers and intrinsic hand muscles, producing ulnar clawing and trouble making a fist, not hand of benediction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Radial nerve lesions cause wrist drop and dorsal hand sensory loss, not loss of wrist flexion or thenar function.
explanation_incorrect.D: Musculocutaneous nerve injury affects elbow flexion and the biceps reflex, not wrist flexion or finger lumbricals.
explanation_incorrect.E: Axillary nerve injury affects shoulder abduction and lateral arm sensation, not hand intrinsic function.

educationalObjective: Proximal median nerve injury from a supracondylar humerus fracture causes hand of benediction on fist-making via LOAF muscle loss and lateral three-and-a-half finger sensory loss.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 40-year-old woman sustains a superficial laceration across the palm of her hand. After healing, she cannot oppose or abduct her thumb, and the thenar eminence appears wasted. Sensation over the thumb and the rest of the hand is normal, and she can still flex her wrist and fingers.
question: Which nerve branch is most likely injured?

options.text: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
Anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve
Recurrent branch of the median nerve

explanation_correct: The recurrent branch of the median nerve arises after the nerve passes through the carpal tunnel and innervates the thenar muscles, namely opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, and flexor pollicis brevis. A superficial palmar laceration can sever this purely motor branch, producing ape hand, or loss of opposition, abduction, and flexion of the thumb with thenar atrophy. Because the recurrent branch is motor and the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the carpal tunnel and travels outside it, sensation is spared, a key localizing feature.

explanation_incorrect.A: The ulnar nerve proper supplies hypothenar and interosseous muscles and medial one-and-a-half finger sensation; a laceration of the recurrent branch spares ulnar structures and sensation.
explanation_incorrect.B: The radial nerve supplies extensors and is not at risk in a superficial palmar laceration; injury would cause wrist drop, not thenar wasting.
explanation_incorrect.C: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve supplies interossei and adductor pollicis, not the thenar OAF muscles; injury would impair finger adduction/abduction rather than thumb opposition.
explanation_incorrect.D: The anterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor forearm branch supplying flexor pollicis longus and the index/middle flexor digitorum profundus; it is not injured by a palm laceration and would not cause thenar atrophy.

educationalObjective: The recurrent motor branch of the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles; its isolated injury causes ape hand with no sensory loss.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 16-year-old boy falls on his outstretched hand and fractures the medial epicondyle of his humerus. He develops weakness of finger abduction and adduction, cannot adduct his thumb, and has numbness in the fifth and medial half of the fourth digit. When asked to extend his fingers, the fourth and fifth digits claw.
question: Which nerve is injured?
explanation_correct: The ulnar nerve (C8-T1) passes posterior to the medial epicondyle at the funny bone, making it vulnerable in medial epicondyle fractures. It innervates the interossei (finger abduction/adduction), adductor pollicis, the medial two lumbricals, and hypothenar muscles, and carries sensation from the ulnar one and a half fingers. Loss of the medial lumbricals, which normally flex MCP and extend IP joints, causes the ulnar claw when the patient extends the fingers. Proximal lesions also cause radial deviation of the wrist on flexion because flexor carpi ulnaris is weakened.

explanation_incorrect.B: Median nerve injury affects the lateral three and a half fingers and LOAF muscles, causing hand of benediction or ape hand, not ulnar clawing or medial one-and-a-half finger sensory loss.
explanation_incorrect.C: Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop and dorsal hand sensory loss, not finger adduction weakness or ulnar clawing.
explanation_incorrect.D: Axillary nerve injury affects the deltoid and lateral arm sensation after surgical neck humerus fractures, not hand intrinsics.
explanation_incorrect.E: Musculocutaneous nerve injury affects elbow flexion and the biceps reflex, not interossei or ulnar sensation.

educationalObjective: Medial epicondyle humerus fractures injure the ulnar nerve, causing ulnar claw, weakened finger adduction/abduction, and ulnar one-and-a-half finger sensory loss.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A medical student reviews a series of humerus fracture cases and notes that nerves are injured in a predictable proximal-to-distal pattern along the bone. A fracture at the surgical neck involves one nerve, a midshaft fracture the next, and a supracondylar fracture the third.
question: Which sequence of nerves corresponds to humerus fractures from proximal to distal?
explanation_correct: Humerus fractures follow the mnemonic ARM from proximal to distal: the surgical neck is associated with the axillary nerve, the midshaft spiral groove with the radial nerve, and the distal humerus/supracondylar region with the median nerve. This pattern reflects the anatomic course of each nerve around the humerus. Recall of this sequence is high yield for localizing nerve lesions by fracture site.

explanation_incorrect.A: Radial, then axillary, then median is incorrect; the radial nerve lies at the midshaft, not the most proximal site.
explanation_incorrect.B: Median, then radial, then axillary reverses the pattern; the median nerve is distal and the axillary is proximal.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ulnar, then radial, then median includes the ulnar nerve, which is injured at the medial epicondyle and is not part of the humeral shaft ARM sequence.
explanation_incorrect.E: Axillary, then median, then radial incorrectly places the median nerve before the radial nerve; the radial nerve at the midshaft comes before the distal median nerve.

educationalObjective: Humerus fractures from proximal to distal injure the axillary, radial, and then median nerves (ARM).
